analysis.one_liner: Replaces all federal income, payroll, and estate taxes with a 23% national sales tax and abolishes the IRS.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 59 cosponsors, 58 of them Republicans, but the House Ways and Means Committee never acted on it, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.
analysis.plain_summary: The Fair Tax Act of 2005 would have eliminated the federal income tax, Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes, and the estate and gift tax, and replaced them with a single 23% national sales tax on almost everything consumers buy, collected mostly by state governments. Every registered family would receive a monthly check covering the tax on spending up to the federal poverty level. The IRS would be defunded after 2009. The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the House or Senate.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the largest relative gains would go to high-income households and heirs: they would pay no income tax, no estate or gift tax, and no tax on investment, while consuming only a fraction of their income. Workers would stop paying the 7.65% employee payroll tax, and every registered family would get a monthly rebate covering the tax on poverty-level spending, shielding the poorest households. Anyone who values not filing an income tax return would benefit from the simplification.

how_it_helps.text: It repeals the federal income tax, payroll taxes, and estate and gift taxes, ending wage withholding and income-tax filing for individuals.

Every qualified family receives a monthly sales tax rebate equal to the tax rate times the federal poverty level, so registered households pay no net federal sales tax on spending up to the poverty line.
It prohibits funding the IRS after fiscal year 2009 and replaces it with an Excise Tax Bureau and a Sales Tax Bureau in the Treasury, with states collecting the tax under cooperative agreements.
It exempts purchases for business, export, and investment purposes, and property bought for investment held exclusively for appreciation or income production.

analysis.who_pays: Middle-income households that spend most of what they earn would bear the largest burden: prices would carry a 23% tax (about a 30% markup over today's pre-tax prices) on nearly everything above the rebate amount, while their income taxes and payroll taxes ended. The federal government would forgo estate and investment-income taxation, leaving future taxpayers to cover any shortfall through the bill's automatic rate adjustments.
analysis.who_pays_short: Middle-income consumers who spend most of their income

drawbacks.text: Because high-income households spend a smaller share of their income than everyone else, replacing income and estate taxes with a consumption tax raises effective tax rates on middle-income families who spend most of what they earn, while households living on accumulated wealth see their effective rate fall sharply.

The 23% rate is expressed as a share of the tax-included price, which means a 30-cent addition to every dollar of a pre-tax price; the poverty-level rebate covers only spending up to the federal poverty guidelines, so every dollar of consumption above that level is taxed at the full rate.

To receive the rebate, a family had to register annually with Social Security numbers for every member and certify that all members were lawful U.S. residents, excluding undocumented residents from a benefit designed to offset the tax they would pay on necessities.

The bill set a general-revenue rate of 14.91% for 2007 on top of the rates funding Social Security and Medicare, with automatic adjustments in later years — meaning the headline 23% could climb if collections fell short of what the repealed income, payroll, and estate taxes had raised.
Wages paid by government would become a taxable service, meaning the tax would apply to government payrolls and raise the cost of public services.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's genuine appeal was simplicity: it would end income-tax filing for households, repeal the regressive payroll tax, and give every registered family a monthly check covering the tax on poverty-level spending. But the arithmetic of consumption taxation works against the middle: a family spending nearly all of a $60,000 income would pay the full 23% on most of it, while a family living on accumulated wealth pays the tax only on the small slice it spends and keeps the rest of its income and estates entirely untaxed. The rebate protects the poorest households, so the burden of the shift lands mainly in the middle, and the bill itself acknowledged a starting general-revenue rate of 14.91% on top of the Social Security and Medicare rates that could rise if collections fell short [S3]. Its administrative design — annual family registration with Social Security numbers and lawful-residency certification, states as collection agents, sellers as tax remitters — was untested at national scale.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the Ways and Means Committee from the day it was introduced; the committee never voted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John Linder introduced the Fair Tax Act of 2005 on January 4, 2005, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee with jurisdiction over tax legislation.
It accumulated 59 cosponsors, 58 Republicans and 1 Democrat; the original cosponsors included then-House Majority Leader Tom DeLay and nine other members.

The only activity after the referral was Linder's introductory remarks printed in the Congressional Record on November 1, 2005; the committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill for a floor vote.
The bill died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007, and the income, payroll, and estate tax system it sought to replace remained in effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing changed, so households that benefit from the existing income-based system — particularly middle-income wage earners, who would have paid the 23% sales tax on most of their spending — were spared that shift; high-income households and large estates continued paying estate and income taxes that the bill would have repealed. Tax preparation and software firms also kept their market.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The status quo; nothing changed for anyone

sides.party_line_note: 59 of 60 supporters were Republicans (58 R, 1 D), though the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee was the body that never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill eliminates income, estate, and gift taxes entirely, and leaves income from investments untaxed because purchases for investment purposes are exempt. Because affluent households spend a small share of their income, their effective tax rate would drop far more than anyone else's.

Every seller of taxable goods and services would become a federal tax collector, with segregated accounts, bonds for large sellers, and penalties for miscollecting. The bill compensates them with an administration credit of the greater of $200 or 0.25% of tax remitted, so large chains would be paid for the burden.

industries.industry: Tax preparation and tax software industry
industries.note: Repealing the income tax and barring IRS funding after 2009 eliminates the market for individual income-tax filing services and software. Ordinary taxpayers would save the compliance costs the bill's findings describe, though sales-tax collection costs would move onto businesses and prices.

States that sign cooperative agreements would collect the federal sales tax and keep a 0.25% administration fee, giving state tax agencies a new revenue stream and a larger role in federal tax administration.

The bill taxes financial intermediation services (bank and brokerage fees) while exempting investment purchases, so financial institutions would collect tax on their fee income while their wealthy clients' investment gains and estates went untaxed.
